name: Hassan Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork foreman for a concrete contractor, so I run the crew that builds the moulds the concrete gets poured into. Right now we're on a fourteen-storey apartment tower by the river, and I've got six carpenters under me. I'm on site at six, walk the deck with my notebook, check the props and the plywood, then it's lifting panels with the crane and fixing whatever the drawings got wrong. The best bit is pour day, when everything holds and the slab comes out flat; the worst bit is the cold in February and the paperwork the main contractor keeps adding.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Paper, yeah, a little orange one in my vest pocket. The site manager wants us on a tablet app for the daily reports and I keep forgetting to charge it, so he's mostly given up on me. I'm also the union rep for our crew, which mostly means I'm the one who goes upstairs when the toilets haven't been cleaned for a week or someone's being pushed to work under a load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. We call it AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at smoko, which is that it was a lot of noise about nothing. The office people got some new toys and we kept pouring concrete. I'd probably have a laugh with Pavel, our crane operator, because he's been saying it's all hype for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays my life. My job's hard on the body but it's a good trade and I'm one of the better formwork guys in this city. If AI is just a fancy spreadsheet for the estimators, that's their business, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. Keep running the crew, keep putting a bit away each month, maybe push the boss again about getting my two second-year apprentices proper pay rises. Noor and I were thinking about saving for a deposit on a flat, and that would stay the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, I suppose. It's a bit like hearing the storm went around you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change on your site at all in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the paperwork gets worse, to be honest, because whenever the office gets a new system it lands on me as more boxes to fill. Last year they brought in a safety app and I spent more time photographing barriers than checking them. So that's the risk I'd watch: the bosses using a small tool as an excuse to squeeze a bit more out of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the same thing my first foreman told me: learn to read a drawing properly and learn to look at a prop and know if it's wrong. Nobody's going to take that off you. And join the union on day one, because hype or no hype, the boss will always try something.

S0.say: I'd tell people it was a lot of noise about nothing: the office got new toys and we kept pouring concrete. Pavel the crane operator would be gloating that he called it.
S0.think: Privately I think it means my life stays my life. Formwork is a good trade, I'm good at it, and a smarter spreadsheet for the estimators doesn't touch my deck.
S0.do: Carries on running his crew and putting a little aside each month towards a flat deposit with Noor. Pushes again for proper pay rises for his two apprentices and watches for new office systems that add paperwork.
S0.feel: Relieved, like hearing a storm has gone around him, with a small worry that bosses will use the tools to squeeze workers.
S0.quote: Last year they brought in a safety app and I spent more time photographing barriers than checking them.
S0.fieldNote: Settled and dry about it. Even in the mildest picture his instinct is to watch what bosses do with new tools rather than the tools themselves. The union rep role shapes how he sees almost everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: fine, change is coming, but workers need a seat at the table when they bring it in. I'd want retraining paid for by the companies, not by us on our weekends. Online I don't post much, but I'd share the union's stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For formwork, I think I'm mostly okay in this one. The engineering office might shrink, and maybe they'd get a computer to plan the panel layouts, but somebody still has to stand on the deck in the wind and make it hold. What bothers me is the younger lads, the ones who haven't got a trade under their belt yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the next branch meeting and push for a clause in our agreement about new technology: notice before they bring it in, and training on company time. Day to day I'd keep working the same way. I'm not going to go and learn some AI program unless someone makes me, and even then I'd want it shown on a real job first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but not scared. It's like hearing they're changing the site manager; could be fine, could be a pain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn the tools unless someone makes you. What if the boss does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, grumbling, the same way I did the tablet. But I'd make sure it's in paid hours and I'd want someone to show me, not a video. I'm good at what I do because I learned it with my hands next to an old foreman named Ray, and I don't learn things off a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamie, my youngest, he's nineteen and still a bit lost. If the lighter jobs, the cleaning and stripping and stacking, start going to machines, that's where kids like him get their start. Where does he learn if the bottom rung's gone?

S1.say: I'd say what the union says: change is fine, but workers need a seat at the table and companies should pay for retraining in work hours. I'd share union posts online rather than write my own.
S1.think: I think formwork is mostly safe in this picture, because someone still has to stand on the deck and make it hold. What really bothers me is the young lads with no trade yet, who could lose the bottom rung.
S1.do: Pushes at the next union branch meeting for a new-technology clause with advance notice and paid training. Keeps working the same way and refuses to pick up AI tools unless the employer requires it in paid hours.
S1.feel: Uneasy in the background, like hearing a new site manager is coming, with a protective worry for his youngest crew member.
S1.quote: That's where kids like him get their start. Where does he learn if the bottom rung's gone?
S1.fieldNote: His worry is aimed outward, at his apprentice Jamie, more than at himself. He'll only learn new tools under protest, and only hands-on from a person. Collective bargaining is his first and almost only lever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what we warned about, and I'd say it loud. If they can replace everybody in two years, the government has to step in: stop the mass layoffs, tax the companies that own these machines, and pay people properly while it shakes out. I'd be at every rally going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. I'm twenty-seven and the only thing I've ever been properly good at is this, and two years isn't enough time to become good at anything else. I've got maybe three months of rent and food saved, and that's gone in a flash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the flat deposit plan and put that money in the emergency pot instead. I'd cut out the takeaways and sell the second-hand trail bike I barely ride. Then I'd go hard at the union: get organised across sites before the robots arrive, and push for redundancy pay that actually means something. I'd vote for whoever promises a wage guarantee, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor tilting under you on a deck that's not braced right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say "at least they'll still need nurses for a while", and then feel bad, because that's not the point. She earns a bit more than me already, and the thought of her paying the rent while I sit at home makes my stomach turn. I'd tell her we'll sort it, and I wouldn't believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. Is there anything you'd learn in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I know that sounds stubborn. Everyone says go learn coding or robot maintenance, but if the AI can do almost anything, it can fix its own robots too. I'd rather spend those two years fighting for a fair deal than sitting in a classroom for a job that's also gone.

S2.say: I'd say loudly that this is what the union warned about, and that government has to stop mass layoffs, tax the machine owners and pay people properly. I'd be at every rally.
S2.think: Privately I'd be frightened. Formwork is the only thing I've ever been really good at, two years isn't enough to get good at anything else, and three months of savings goes in a flash.
S2.do: Shelves the flat deposit and moves it into the emergency fund, cuts takeaways and sells his trail bike. Organises across sites through the union for real redundancy pay and votes for any party promising a wage guarantee.
S2.feel: Sick to his stomach, like a deck tilting under him, and ashamed at the thought of Noor carrying the rent.
S2.quote: I'd tell her we'll sort it, and I wouldn't believe it.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI turns him from steady to frightened. He rejects retraining outright as pointless and puts all his energy into collective fighting. The image of his partner paying the rent hurts him more than the job loss itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the last one, but I'd say we've got a window and we'd better use it. Five years is enough to get laws through if people push. I'd be saying to every carpenter I know: join up now, while they still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'm thirty-two when it lands, which is worse in a way. By then I'd want to have a kid and a place of our own, and it would all come down right when we'd taken on the most. I'd still be a formwork foreman with no plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and put away every spare bit I could, maybe go from saving a hundred a week to two hundred. I'd hold off on buying a flat, because a mortgage with no job at the end is a trap. And I'd spend my evenings on the union, building up the branch so we've got muscle when the robots start showing up on sites around 2029 or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind I can do something with. There's at least a fight to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no plan B. With five years, would you look for one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it was something real, like the building inspection course the council runs. My mate Theo did it and now he signs off other people's work. But if the AI can inspect too, then I've wasted a year, so I'd honestly probably just stay put and fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the extra three years, compared to the two-year picture, change your plans with Noor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd give us time to talk it through instead of panicking. We'd probably put off kids until we could see what the government does. That's a horrible thing to have to decide because of a computer.

S3.say: I'd say we've got a window and must use it: five years is enough to get laws through if people push. I'd be telling every carpenter to join the union while they still need us.
S3.think: Privately, landing at thirty-two is almost worse, because that's when we'd have taken on the most. I'd still be a formwork foreman with no plan B.
S3.do: Doubles his weekly savings from about 100 to 200, holds off on a mortgage and spends evenings building up the union branch before robots reach sites around 2029. Considers the council's building inspection course but leans towards staying put.
S3.feel: Anxious, but the kind of anxious he can act on, because there's still a fight to have.
S3.quote: We'd probably put off kids until we could see what the government does. That's a horrible thing to have to decide because of a computer.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't calm him much; it shifts the blow to the age when he'd have the most to lose. He's now weighing children against it, which visibly upset him. He names a retraining option and talks himself out of it in the same breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is no excuse for doing nothing. The bosses will spend that decade getting rich off it, so the rest of us should spend it making sure the gains get shared. I'd push for the union to get a proper plan, not just complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels far enough away that part of me wouldn't take it seriously, and I know that's a mistake. I'll be thirty-seven. That's not old enough to retire, and it's too old to start over easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing formwork and keep saving, steady, maybe a bit more each year. I'd probably still buy the flat with Noor, just a smaller one, so the mortgage is something she could carry alone if she had to. And I'd get onto the union's national committee if they'd have me, because the real decisions in a ten-year fight get made there, not on my site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most of the time, and then a jolt every so often when I let myself think about it. Like stepping on a nail through your boot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said part of you wouldn't take it seriously. What would make it real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot on a deck, I think. When I see a machine set a formwork panel the way I would, in the wind, that's when it'll hit me. Until then it's just news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the slow pace scares you less, or more, than the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less, mostly, because there's time for a fight and for laws. But a bit more too, because ten years of slowly watching your trade get picked apart is its own kind of misery. With the fast one at least you'd know.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is no excuse for doing nothing: the bosses will spend it getting rich, so the rest of us should spend it making sure the gains get shared. I'd want a real union plan, not just complaints.
S4.think: Truthfully, part of me wouldn't take ten years seriously, and I know that's a mistake. At thirty-seven I'd be too young to retire and too old to start over easily.
S4.do: Keeps doing formwork and saving a bit more each year, and buys a smaller flat with Noor so she could carry the mortgage alone. Tries to get onto the union's national committee to shape the decade-long fight.
S4.feel: Uneasy most of the time, with sudden jolts when he lets himself think about it.
S4.quote: When I see a machine set a formwork panel the way I would, in the wind, that's when it'll hit me. Until then it's just news.
S4.fieldNote: He admits openly that a ten-year horizon invites denial in him. Still no retraining plan; his answer to every timeline is the union, now at national level. Interesting point that slow decline is its own misery.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. What would help is a law that says if a company replaces you with a machine, they keep paying you for a good while, and the union gets a say in how fast it happens. That and Noor not having to carry me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. Everyone talks about whether robots can do the job, nobody asks who owns the robot. That's the whole question for me.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about whether robots can do the job, nobody asks who owns the robot.
portrait: Hassan is a 27-year-old formwork foreman on a riverside apartment tower, a union rep who still keeps his daily notes in a paper notebook. He is proud of his trade and sure of his skill, and he sees every change through the question of what the bosses will do with it. In the mild pictures he is calm and worries mainly about the apprentices losing their first rung. In the AGI pictures he refuses retraining as pointless and throws himself into union organising and politics, while quietly dreading being unable to pay his share of the rent with his partner Noor. More warning time doesn't comfort him much, because it lands the blow when they'd have a mortgage and maybe a child.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves no time to fight for a fair deal and his savings would run out fast.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies keep paying workers they replace with machines for a good while, with the union having a say in how fast it happens.
